title: DataBook
description: A worked example of how one table becomes an interactive data report.

notes: Values are generated by y = 2^x. The example contains no observed data.

rows.body:
## What does doubling look like?

Start with one unit and double it at each step. After four steps there are 16 units. After eight there are 256. Hover over the curve or use the arrow keys once the chart is focused to inspect the points.

This is a **DataBook**, an interactive report that puts Markdown, charts, and the queries behind them in one project. The **Example** page tells the story. **How it works** explains the files and authoring workflow. [View the source on GitHub](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook).

## Zoom in on the early steps

The first five values run from 1 to 16. They look nearly flat on the full chart because its vertical axis also has to fit 256. Here the same chart component receives only rows with `x ≤ 4`, and the vertical axis rescales to fit them.

## Follow a chart back to its data

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| [`canonical.json`](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/src/data/canonical.json) | A typed table with one row per doubling step |
| [`rows.json`](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/src/data/rows.json) | Pages, tabs, Markdown, and each chart's query |
| [`ExponentialCurve.tsx`](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/src/charts/ExponentialCurve.tsx) | The React component that draws the query result |

The query engine filters, groups, bins, aggregates, and sorts the canonical table in the browser. The early-steps chart uses a filter with `column: x`, `op: lte`, and `value: 4`, then sorts by `x` in ascending order.

Run `npm run print-block -- early-steps` locally to inspect the exact rows it passes to the chart. The chart below references the original block by ID, so it shares its query and rendering code.

## Make a book of your own

Clone the [DataBook repository](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook), run `npm ci`, then run `npm run dev`. The [README](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook#readme) walks through setup and the [DataBook skill](https://github.com/kdopenshaw/databook/blob/main/SKILL.md) describes the workflow for coding agents.

1. Define the grain and columns of your canonical table. Document your assumptions in `src/data/understanding.md`.
2. Add narrative and chart queries to `src/data/rows.json`. Write chart components in `src/charts/`.
3. Run `npm run ok` to validate the book and check that each chart query returns rows. Run `npm run build` to make a shareable static site.

**Try an edit.** Click in the prose on this tab and type to edit it. Use the sidebar and tabs to organize the book. Edits to this hosted demo stay in this browser. When running locally with Vite, edits are written to `rows.json`.

**Ask for a chart locally.** With the Codex CLI installed and signed in, add a prompt row and describe the chart. DataBook runs Codex in the project so it can add the chart component and its query.
